candidates.solves: Counting owned items (e.g., pets) as of a target date fails when ownership is stored as a profile or state memory rather than an event, or when named instances appear only in plans or other memories and are not followed up with targeted searches, causing the agent to miss instances or count intentions as possessions.

payload.name: Search Relationship and Naming Events for Group Members
payload.description: When a question asks for the names of a person's pets, family, or group members and the first search returns activity memories without names, include relationship memories and search naming/acquisition events.
content: When a question asks for the names or identities of a person's pets, family, or group members, include relationship memory kinds (pet, family, member_of) in the search, not only event and state.

If the first search returns activity memories without names, run targeted searches for acquisition or definition events such as adopted, bought, received, named, or welcomed, combined with the person and the entity type.
Answer only from retrieved evidence; if only some names are supported, report those with their supporting memories and do not infer missing names from group size.
Stop after one relationship-kind pass and one acquisition-event pass; avoid searching indefinitely for every possible name.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask for the names of a person's pets, family members, or group members often miss evidence because generic activity-based searches return no names and relationship memory kinds are excluded from retrieval.

payload.name: Search relationship memories for owned-entity attributes
payload.description: When a question asks how old a person's pet, animal, or owned item is, include relationship memories in the search; ages and attributes are often stored in the ownership relationship memory, not only in profile/state memories.
content: When asked for the age(s) of someone's pet(s), animal(s), or owned item(s), do not restrict retrieval to profile/state memories; include relationship memories because ownership records often contain the entity's age or other attributes.

If the first search returns no direct age, run one additional targeted search using the owner's name plus the entity names and age terms (e.g., 'old', 'years old', 'age') with memory_kinds including relationship; inspect any ownership memory that names the entities.
Stop once a memory directly states the age(s); answer with the stated ages and cite the memory. Do not derive ages from unrelated events or make estimates unless no direct evidence exists.

candidates.solves: Age and attribute questions about a person's pets or owned items often fail because the target values are stored inside relationship memories (e.g., an ownership record that also states the pet's age), while the agent searches only profile/state memories and stops. This Skill ensures relationship memories are included for such attribute-of-owned-entity queries and provides a focused follow-up search before giving up.

payload.name: Search family additions including pets
payload.description: When a question asks who or what was added to or joined a named person's family/group within a time period, include pet-adoption and acquisition terms in retrieval, not only human family-member names.
content: When a question asks about a new addition to someone's family or group (e.g., 'new addition', 'joined the family', 'welcomed'), treat the addition as possibly a pet: run targeted hybrid/keyword searches combining the person's name with acquisition terms such as 'adopted', 'got', 'welcomed', 'new pet', 'brought home', and the time period if given.
Do not restrict family-member searches to human relations; if initial people-focused searches return no matching family member, search pet/animal adoption memories before answering.

If a matching adoption/acquisition memory is found, verify the entity's name and the event date from that memory; stop after one or two targeted addition searches return a consistent answer or after both people-focused and pet-focused searches exhaust.

candidates.solves: Questions asking who or what was added to a person's family within a time period often fail because retrieval is limited to human family-member names and misses pet adoptions stored as event memories.

payload.name: Retrieve Symbolic Gifts by Giver and Meaning
payload.description: Use when a question asks what symbolic gift, meaningful object, or memento a person received from another person (e.g., a mother), especially for two named people; expand search with giving-relationship and symbolic-meaning terms.
content: When a question asks what symbolic gift, meaningful object, or memento someone received from another person, do not rely only on the words 'gift' or 'symbolic'. Run hybrid/keyword searches that combine the giver and receiver with relationship terms ('given by', 'received from', 'from <giver>') and symbolic-meaning terms ('represents', 'reminder', 'in memory of', 'memento', 'keepsake').

If the combined query returns evidence for only one named person, run separate searches for each person (e.g., '<name> given by <giver>', '<name> represents/reminder') and include all memory kinds (preference, event, profile) since these objects are often stored under predicates like symbol, memento, or relationship.

Stop when each person's object is supported by a memory that explicitly names both the giver and the object's symbolic meaning, or after two diverse per-person searches per person yield no new relevant memories.

candidates.solves: A question asks what symbolic gifts or meaningful objects two or more people received from a specific giver. Generic 'gift/symbolic' queries miss memories that express the relationship and symbolism with different wording, and combined queries may surface only one person.

payload.name: Search relationship memories for pet ages
payload.description: When a question asks how old a person's pet or animal is, include relationship memories in the search and query by pet names and age terms before concluding no information.
content: When a question asks for the age(s) of a person's pet(s) or animal(s) (e.g., 'How old is X's cat/dog?'), do not restrict memory_kinds to profile/state; include relationship memories because pet ownership and ages are often stored there.
Run a hybrid/structured search with the owner's name, pet type/name(s), and age phrases ('years old', 'age'), using memory_kinds=['profile','state','relationship'].
If the first search returns no age evidence, inspect relationship memories that list the person's pets for named individuals, then run one targeted search for each pet name plus 'age'/'years old'.
Stop once ages are found or after one additional targeted search per pet returns nothing; do not answer 'No information available' after a single profile/state-only search.

candidates.solves: When a user asks for the age of a pet or animal (e.g., 'How old are Deborah's cats?'), the Access Agent often restricts searches to profile/state memories and misses relationship memories that contain the pet details and ages, then wrongly answers 'No information available'.

payload.name: Search Event Evidence for Shared Possessions
payload.description: When a question asks what similar item or collectible two people possess, search each person for acquisition events (signed, received, gifted, teammates gave) in addition to ownership states before answering.
content: For questions asking what similar item or collectible two people own, run separate searches for each person covering both possession phrasings (owns, has, possesses) and acquisition-event phrasings (signed, received, gifted, given, teammates gave, awarded).
Treat an event in which an item was signed, received, or given to a person as evidence of possession for commonality questions, not only state/profile memories.
Before answering, ensure a candidate overlap is supported by evidence from both named people; stop after two or three query variants per person if no new acquisition events surface.

candidates.solves: Questions comparing what two people own or collect often miss relevant evidence because ownership may be recorded in event memories (e.g., an item signed or given to them) rather than a state memory saying 'owns'. Retrieval queries using only 'owns' or 'collectible' fail to surface these acquisition events. This skill generalizes the need to broaden per-person searches to event phrasings and treat received/signed/gifted items as possession evidence.

payload.name: Enumerate Visited Place Categories
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds of places (cafes, parks, shelters, events) a person or two named people have checked out or visited, and one generic places query returns sparse results.
content: When a question asks what kinds of places a person or pair has visited/checked out, do not stop after one generic 'places' query; run targeted hybrid or keyword searches for each likely place category (dining, outdoor/hiking, pet-related, entertainment, events) with the person's name and category terms.

Search across event, plan, and state memories, but count a place as checked out only when a memory explicitly states a visit, attendance, or discovery (visited, went to, attended, discovered); exclude plans, intentions, and still-searching-for statements.
Stop once the distinct place types named across searches have all been covered, or after at most three targeted category searches beyond the initial query.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask what kinds of places a person (or pair) has visited or checked out around a city often fail when one generic 'places' query retrieves only a few memories; this skill requires searching by place category and excluding planned or sought places so the answer is a complete, evidence-supported enumeration.

payload.name: Complete all visited places for enumeration questions
payload.description: When a question asks for all cities/places a person has visited (e.g., 'which cities has X visited?'), use this to avoid stopping after one destination.
content: When a question asks for all cities/places a person has visited, treat it as list completion: do not answer after the first location memory; continue searching for additional destinations.

Use travel-verb queries in addition to 'visited', including 'trip to', 'traveled to', 'went to', and 'vacation', and search event, state, and profile memories; do not rely only on the word 'city' in the query.

After each found destination, run at least one more search for another destination (e.g., person name plus 'trip' or 'also went to') before concluding; stop when a search returns no new unique destination or after at most two extra searches.

candidates.solves: Access agents often stop after the first location for questions asking for all cities/places a person has visited, missing additional destination memories worded with 'trip' or 'traveled to'. This adds an enumeration-completion step with bounded extra searches.

payload.name: Exhaustive Location List Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for a list of locations/items (e.g., 'which cities does X mention visiting?'), use this skill to retrieve all distinct answers before responding.
content: When a question asks for a list of locations/items, treat it as an enumeration task: run multiple searches with alternative travel/location phrasings (traveled to, went to, visited, trip to, game/match/concert in, excited about [city]) rather than only the words from the question.

Do not require all named persons to co-occur in a memory; the target attribute belongs to the primary subject, so search primarily by that subject plus location terms, and include memories that mention the subject without the conversation partner.
Search across memory kinds (event, plan, state, preference) and do not restrict to travel-themed memories; cities can appear incidentally (e.g., 'basketball game in Seattle').

Continue searching until no new distinct locations appear or after at most three additional searches beyond the first; if the question is plural, expect multiple answers and do not stop after the first match.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a list of locations or items (e.g., which cities a person visited or mentioned), retrieval often stops after finding one answer or over-constrains the search to all named entities, causing missing items. This skill ensures complete enumeration by running varied location-oriented searches until no new distinct items appear.

payload.name: Motivation Retrieval Across Memory Kinds
payload.description: Use when a question asks what motivates or drives a named person to maintain a health, fitness, or other goal, and the motivation may be stored outside profile memories.
content: For questions asking what motivates or drives a person, do not restrict searches to the profile memory kind; run at least one hybrid search that includes preference and state kinds, because motivations are commonly stored there.

After the first broad search, run a follow-up using concrete variants of the motivator (e.g., family, adventure, tracker, goal) in addition to words like 'motivation' and 'reason', since memories often name the specific motivator rather than the abstract category.
If searches return no evidence, inspect preference and state memories with the person's name before answering 'no information'; do not conclude absence from a profile-only search.
Stop once each distinct motivation named in the question or reference is supported by evidence; avoid exhaustive expansions.

candidates.solves: Questions about why a person does something (motivation, reason, drive) frequently fail because agents restrict retrieval to profile memories, while motivations appear in preference and state memories. This skill directs searches across relevant memory kinds and concrete motivator terms.

payload.name: Multi-method promotion retrieval
payload.description: Use when a question asks how someone promoted, marketed, advertised, or grew a business/store, and the first search returns only one or two promotional actions. Apply before answering to enumerate distinct methods.
content: After an initial search for a 'how did X promote/market/advertise' question, treat the answer as needing enumeration: run at least one follow-up hybrid/BM25 search using the subject plus alternative promotion terms such as 'collaborated with', 'limited edition', 'video', 'presentation', 'offers', 'campaign', 'social media', 'event', or 'partnership'.

When reviewing event memories, extract every distinct promotional action described (e.g., collaborations, product lines, media presentations, discounts/offers), not only the first or highest-scoring result.
Stop when a follow-up search returns no new promotional actions for the same subject, or after at most two additional searches; do not exhaustively retrieve all business history.
If the retrieved memories include a plan or intention rather than a completed action, do not count it as a promotion unless another memory confirms the action occurred.

candidates.solves: Improves recall for questions asking how a person or business promoted, marketed, or advertised a product or store, where the expected answer is a list of several distinct promotional activities. Prevents premature single-answer responses by requiring follow-up searches with varied promotion-related terms and enumerating all found promotional actions before answering.

payload.name: Class Course Workshop and Group Enrollment Retrieval
payload.description: Use when a question asks what classes, courses, workshops, trainings, or groups a person has joined, taken, attended, or participated in.
content: When asked about classes, courses, workshops, trainings, or groups a person has joined, taken, or participated in, run searches across memory kinds event, plan, preference, and profile; do not restrict to event/plan alone.

Use varied enrollment/participation phrasing such as 'signed up', 'took', 'started', 'attended', 'joined', 'participated', 'involved in', 'workshop', 'course', 'class', and 'group', combined with the person's name or topic.

Merge results across searches and stop once all distinct classes/groups the question asks about are found or one additional targeted search returns no new candidates; do not require the exact word 'class' or 'group' to appear in a memory.

candidates.solves: Agent misses classes/courses/workshops/groups when retrieval is anchored on the question's noun phrases and restricted to event/plan memory kinds, even though such memberships may be stored in profile/preference memories and phrased as 'signed up', 'took', 'involved in' or 'workshop'.

payload.name: Past Activity Retrieval with Action Verbs
payload.description: When a question asks what someone has done with a person, pet, or object, search with concrete activity verbs and synonyms, and answer only from memories showing the action actually occurred.
content: For questions asking what a person has done with something, expand the query with concrete action verbs and gerunds related to the domain (e.g., walk, hiking, play, train, visit, take care of) and run targeted searches for each likely action, not just one broad natural-language query.

Treat only memories that indicate the action was actually performed (past or ongoing events, habits, or stated experiences) as evidence; do not present plans, intentions, considerations, or other future-oriented memories as things the person has done.

If a retrieved memory describes the activity with different wording than the question, accept it and include it in the answer; when the first search misses a likely action, retry with synonyms and variants.
Stop once each likely activity is either supported by a memory or has been searched for without success; do not exhaustively enumerate all possible activities.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what a person has done with someone or something, the agent often relies on one broad semantic search, misses concrete past activities stored under different wording, and answers with future intentions or plans. This skill guides retrieval to use action-specific verbs and synonyms and to separate performed actions from planned or intended ones.

payload.name: Concrete Noun Searches for Alternative Career Clues
payload.description: When a question asks about alternative careers or next paths and broad hobby/interest searches return only the current-role domain, use concrete non-work terms (pets, animals, nature, art, sports, volunteering) in follow-up searches before answering.
content: When a question asks about an alternative career or what someone could do after a current role, and initial 'hobbies/interests' searches return only memories tied to the current role, run follow-up hybrid searches using the person's name plus concrete non-work nouns that could appear in stored activity/pet-care memories (e.g., pets, animals, nature, sport, art, volunteering, cooking).
Include memory kinds event and state in these follow-up searches; pet care, hobbies, and passions are often stored as events or states without the words 'hobby', 'interest', or 'career'.
If a concrete domain surfaces (e.g., animal care, nature), search that domain plus the person's name to retrieve knowledge and enjoyment memories that can support a career suggestion.
Stop after two concrete-term searches yield no new relevant memories, or once the alternative career is supported by visible evidence.

candidates.solves: Alternative-career questions often fail because broad hobby/interest searches miss concrete activity or pet-care memories stored without the words 'hobby', 'interest', or 'career'. The fix is to follow up with concrete non-work nouns and include event and state memories so knowledge and enjoyment in specific domains can surface.

payload.name: Concrete Project Retrieval for Broad Category Questions
payload.description: When a question asks what kind/types of projects or work a person has done in a broad category, use after initial retrieval to check specificity and search for named examples without the category term.
content: When a question asks what kind of projects or work a person has done in a broad category (e.g., engineering, research, art), do not stop after the first retrieval returns generic memories that only mention the category without concrete project names or topics.

If the retrieved memories are vague about the actual project subject, run a follow-up search that omits the broad category keyword and uses the person's name plus outcome/action terms such as 'designed', 'built', 'developed', 'created', 'prototype', 'system', 'device', 'working on', or 'completed'.
Include memory kinds 'event', 'plan', 'state', and 'profile' in the follow-up, and inspect returned memories for concrete project descriptions (e.g., named products, systems, or technologies).
Stop after one additional targeted search that yields no new concrete project names; do not expand exhaustively.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what kinds or types of projects a person has worked on in a broad field (e.g., engineering, research, art), retrieval can over-anchor on the field name and return generic category-tagged memories while missing concrete project examples that actually define the types. This skill prompts the agent to verify that retrieved memories name specific projects and, when they are too vague, to run a follow-up search using the person's name and outcome/action terms without the broad category keyword.

payload.name: Supplement Activity Retrieval with Event Kinds
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone does to supplement, complement, or add to a named activity, and initial results exclude event/plan memories.
content: When a question asks what someone does to supplement, complement, or add to a named primary activity, do not restrict memory kinds to profile and relationship; include event and plan because the supplement is often recorded as a training routine, class, or ongoing practice.

Run at least one follow-up query that omits the primary activity name and uses the person's name with supplement-oriented terms such as 'training', 'workout', 'practice', 'class', 'routine', 'strength', 'yoga', 'gym', or 'exercise'.

Do not answer from a single search result that only mentions the primary activity or an unrelated activity (e.g., community service); continue searching until a memory explicitly describes an additional activity, or two distinct searches yield no new supplement.

candidates.solves: This solves retrieval failures where a question about supplementary activities returns only profile/relationship memories and misses event memories that record the actual supplementing activities (e.g., yoga, strength training).

payload.name: Rewarding-experience outcome synonym retrieval
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone recently participated in or did that was rewarding, fulfilling, or positive without naming a specific activity, and the initial retrieval returns memories containing the word 'rewarding' but none directly answers. Apply before answering.
content: If the question asks about a rewarding or fulfilling experience without naming the activity, do not settle for memories that merely contain the word 'rewarding'; the target event may describe the outcome instead (e.g., positive feedback, recognition, achievement, progress toward goals).

Run at least one follow-up search combining the person's name with outcome and activity synonyms such as 'presented', 'presentation', 'conference', 'positive feedback', 'achievement', 'recognized', 'success', 'confirmed', 'on the right track', and, if supported, filter to event memories with predicates like achievement.

When evaluating candidates, accept an event memory as evidence of a rewarding experience if it describes positive outcomes or goal confirmation even without the exact word 'rewarding', and prefer the most recent such event.
Stop once a directly supporting event memory is found or after two targeted follow-up searches yield nothing; do not exhaustively enumerate all possibly rewarding activities.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what someone recently participated in or did that was rewarding or fulfilling, a single search using the literal word 'rewarding' can over-anchor and miss event memories that describe the same experience through outcome language such as positive feedback, recognition, achievement, or progress toward goals. This skill guides follow-up searches with outcome synonyms and event/predicate filters so the correct recent activity is retrieved and selected.

payload.name: Stress Relief Retrieval: Comfort Items and Indirect Attribution
payload.description: Use when a question asks what relieves a person's stress, relaxes them, or helps them unwind, and the answer may include comfort foods, guilty pleasures, or activities mentioned through another person's recommendation.
content: When asked what relieves a person's stress, search for comfort foods and guilty pleasures in addition to activities and places, using terms like 'snacks', 'sweets', 'candy', 'soda', 'comfort food', 'treat', and 'guilty' with the person's name.

Do not discard a memory about another person's stress reliever if it says the queried person suggested or recommended it; run a targeted search for the queried person's own use of that activity before excluding it.

Before answering, verify each distinct stress reliever is attributed to the queried person by a supporting memory; include comfort items and indirect suggestions only when the memory or a follow-up search supports the queried person's use or preference.

candidates.solves: Questions about stress relief often return only activity/place preferences and miss comfort foods, guilty pleasures, or indirect recommendations, leading to incomplete answers. This skill directs retrieval to include non-activity comforts and to verify indirect attributions before finalizing.

payload.name: Motivation and trigger retrieval for why-start questions
payload.description: When a question asks why someone decided to start, launch, or begin an activity or business, use this Skill to retrieve both personal passion and precipitating trigger events before answering.
content: When the question asks why someone decided to start/launch/begin an activity or business, run at least one extra search combining the person's name with motivation terms ('passion', 'love', 'always wanted', 'dream', 'inspired') and at least one search with trigger terms ('lost job', 'left job', 'opportunity', 'decided', 'finally', 'after') if the initial results lack either.

When reviewing retrieved memories, treat both the person's expressed interest/passion and any triggering life event as evidence for the decision; do not answer from a single memory if it covers only one side.
Stop as soon as you have at least one memory covering the motivation and one covering the trigger, or after 2-3 targeted searches; do not exhaustively retrieve all business-related events.

candidates.solves: Answers for 'why did X start/launch Y' often require both a personal motivation (interest/passion) and a triggering event (e.g., job loss, opportunity). The default single-search flow may retrieve only one side, leading to incomplete answers. This Skill adds targeted searches for both dimensions before answering.

payload.name: Prioritize Enduring Interest Over One-Off Activity
payload.description: When a question asks what passion or interest connects a person with other people, use it to choose among returned hobby/activity memories.
content: When a question asks what passion or interest connects a person with other people, search for stated passions and preferences using terms like 'passionate about', 'loves', 'favorite', 'genre', 'fan of', in addition to hobby terms.

If multiple hobby/event memories are returned, prioritize an enduring interest, genre, or fan community over a single activity or club membership; prefer memories that explicitly link the interest to meeting people, friends, or a worldwide community.
If the strongest evidence is an event such as a party, marathon, or conference, answer with the underlying interest or fandom it reflects rather than the event itself.
Stop after two targeted searches and one preference-selection pass; do not exhaustively list all hobbies.

candidates.solves: Distinguishes an enduring interest/fandom from a one-off activity when a question asks which passion connects a person with others, choosing the underlying preference over a club or event.

payload.name: Search Event and Plan Kinds for Replacement Activities
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did or planned instead of, rather than, or as an alternative to a named activity, include event and plan memory kinds and search with replacement-oriented terms.
content: Do not restrict retrieval to memory kinds profile and relationship when looking for an alternative or replacement activity; include event and plan, because planned replacements are often stored as event or plan memories.
Run at least one query that combines the person's name with replacement-oriented terms such as 'plan', 'play', 'together', 'instead', or 'want to try' and omits the superseded activity.

If the first results only mention the superseded activity or another subject, run one more query using candidate activity nouns from retrieved memories before answering; stop once a same-subject memory explicitly describes the replacement.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what activity someone did or planned instead of a named activity, retrieval can fail because searches are restricted to profile and relationship memory kinds and remain anchored on the superseded activity, while the actual replacement is stored as an event or plan memory with different activity terms.

payload.name: Retrieve preference memories for activity-enhancement questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what type of music, food, or other item a person finds helpful, prefers, or uses during a named activity (e.g., yoga, workout, studying).
content: When the question pairs a person with an activity and a category (e.g., music during yoga), do not restrict search to profile memories; explicitly include preference (and state) memory kinds, since the answer is often stored as a preference.

Run the initial hybrid search using the person's name, the activity, and the category keyword (e.g., music, food, playlist); if no direct match, expand with terms like 'during', 'while', 'for', 'favorite', 'prefers'.
If a preference memory is found that directly states the item and activity, stop searching and answer from it; do not run additional exploratory searches.

candidates.solves: Access fails when a question asks what type of thing a person finds helpful during a named activity, because retrieval is restricted to profile memories and misses preference memories that contain the answer.

payload.name: Knowledge-Sharing Activity Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone does to share knowledge, teach, mentor, or help others develop, use concrete activity verbs when searching and supplement after finding one activity.
content: When a question asks how someone shares knowledge, teaches, mentors, or helps others develop, do not search only the abstract phrase 'share knowledge'. Run hybrid searches using concrete activity terms such as 'gives seminars', 'teaches', 'mentors', 'coaches', 'trains', 'workshops', 'presents', and 'helps others'.
Include memory kinds event and plan; knowledge-sharing actions are often stored as specific events or planned sessions rather than as general knowledge statements.
After finding one activity, run at least one additional search with a different concrete activity verb before answering, because a person may share knowledge in multiple distinct ways.
Stop after two or three distinct query attempts yield no new activity, and answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: Access retrieval misses memories of concrete knowledge-sharing activities (seminars, teaching, mentoring) when the question is phrased abstractly as 'share knowledge'. The agent searches only variations of the abstract phrase and does not target specific activity verbs, so distinct supporting memories are left out of the answer.

payload.name: Current-activity title retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is reading, watching, listening to, or playing (e.g., 'What novel is X reading?'), include activity-specific query variants and run a structured event search for that predicate before answering no information.
content: When the question asks what a person is reading, watching, listening to, or playing (e.g., 'What novel is X reading?'), include query variants that pair the person's name with the activity verb and the object type: 'reading novel', 'watching show', 'listening to album', 'playing game'.

If the initial hybrid search does not surface a memory with a specific title, run one structured search filtered to memory_kind=event, subject=<person>, and predicate in (read, watch, listen, play) before answering 'No information available'.
Stop after that structured search returns no relevant memory; do not expand to unrelated activities or topics.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what a person is currently reading, watching, listening to, or playing, the initial generic search often fails to surface the specific title because the memory may be combined with unrelated content or the predicate is not matched. This skill ensures activity-specific retrieval is performed before concluding no information.

payload.name: Affective Hobby Evidence Search
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a person's hobbies or interests, especially when explicit hobby lists are missing or partial.
content: When answering hobby/interest questions, also search preference memories using affective-emotion verbs: 'finds comfort in', 'brings joy', 'loves', 'passionate about', 'enjoys', 'happy when', because stable hobbies are often stored with emotional language rather than as a hobby list.
Prefer preference memories as evidence for stable hobbies; do not list one-off events (e.g., a single class, one DIY project) as hobbies unless the memory shows recurrence or an ongoing interest.
Run at most one or two affective-phrasing searches after the initial hobby search, and stop once the explicit hobby list is covered or no new distinct hobbies appear.

candidates.solves: Hobby questions often fail when preferences are stored using emotional language (comfort, joy, love) and when one-off events are over-listed as hobbies. This Skill guides retrieval to affective preference memories and filters out non-recurring events.

payload.name: Retrieve alternate focus areas for 'besides' questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides an explicit main activity (e.g., studying, work), search for other life domains such as relationships, hobbies, and social activities.
content: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides an explicit main activity (e.g., studying, work), do not stop at generic self-care or non-study queries; add targeted searches for relationship and hobby terms like 'partner', 'relationship', 'together', 'hobby', and 'activity'.
Include event and preference memory kinds in these searches, and inspect memories that mention the person alongside another name or a joint activity even if they do not literally contain 'focus'.
Stop after two or three distinct query attempts once a plausible non-primary focus area is found; answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what someone has been focusing on lately besides a primary activity (e.g., studying or work), retrieval can miss relationship and hobby memories if queries are anchored only to the negated activity. This skill guides complementary searches across other life domains.

payload.name: Enhancement Props Retrieval for Practice Questions
payload.description: When a question asks how someone enhances, improves, or creates atmosphere for a named practice (e.g., yoga, meditation, workout), and initial results show only routines or benefits, search for concrete sensory props before answering.
content: When a question asks how someone enhances or sets the atmosphere for a named practice, do not anchor retrieval only to the activity name plus 'enhance', 'improve', or 'practice'.

Run a follow-up hybrid search for concrete sensory/ambiance terms likely to appear in the answer, such as 'music', 'candles', 'essential oils', 'scents', 'incense', 'lighting', or 'atmosphere', combined with the person's name.
Include memory kinds 'preference' and 'event' in these follow-up searches; enhancement props are often stored as favorite scents/music or as details of a past practice event.

If the first search returns only routine or benefit memories, treat that as over-anchoring and run these concrete-term searches before answering; stop once the answer components are supported or after two or three diverse searches yield no such memories.

candidates.solves: Questions about how people enhance or improve a recurring practice often expect concrete sensory or ambiance props (e.g., music, candles, essential oils, scents) that are stored in preference or event memories. Retrieval anchored only on the activity name plus 'enhance/improve' surfaces general routine or benefit memories and misses these answer-bearing memories.

payload.name: Compound Activity Retrieval with Constraint Omission
payload.description: Use when a question asks for an activity or pastime combining a person's enjoyment with another condition (indoor, pet, another person), and initial results only match one side of the condition.
content: After the first search, run at least one follow-up query using only enjoyment/hobby terms ('hobby', 'enjoys', 'interested in', 'started', 'likes to') and deliberately omit all additional-constraint keywords such as indoor, pet, or the other person.
Include memory kinds preference, event, and plan in these follow-ups; a hobby can be stored as a routine, plan, or preference without mentioning the extra condition.

If a retrieved hobby can reasonably satisfy the extra condition (e.g., an indoor-friendly hobby or a hobby that can involve a pet), treat that as the best candidate; otherwise answer from the best available evidence and do not invent connections.
Stop after one such follow-up and one combination check; avoid further expansion.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an activity that a person would enjoy while also satisfying another condition, such as being indoors, involving a pet, or pleasing someone else, retrieval often over-anchors on the extra condition and misses the person's stored hobby or preference that is recorded without mentioning that condition.

payload.name: Opening or Launch Object Retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is working on opening, launching, or starting, and initial retrieval returns only generic project or business memories, use opening-focused queries and require evidence explicitly naming the thing being opened before answering.
content: When the question asks what a person is working on opening, launching, or starting, include query variants with the person's name and opening-focused terms such as 'opening', 'launch', 'grand opening', 'preparing to open', and 'opening night'; add a domain term if the question or memory context suggests one (e.g., studio, store, restaurant).

Before answering from a generic 'business plan', 'project', or 'work in progress' memory, verify it explicitly identifies the object being opened; if it does not, run one additional targeted search combining the person's name with opening-focused terms and inspect event/plan memories whose predicate or object indicates a launch.

Stop after that targeted search: if it returns a memory explicitly naming the thing being opened, answer from it; if it still does not, answer no information or the best supported evidence without expanding further.

candidates.solves: Questions phrased as 'what is X working on opening/launching/starting?' are often answered from generic work-in-progress memories such as 'business plan' or 'project', even when a more specific memory names the entity being opened. This skill ensures retrieval explicitly targets the object of the opening and that the answer is grounded in evidence naming that object.

payload.name: Thematic focus retrieval for sessions and retreats
payload.description: Use when a question asks what the main focus, theme, lesson, realization, or takeaway was from a session, retreat, workshop, or event, and initial results show only the activity/event name.
content: When a question asks about the main focus/theme/lesson/takeaway/realization from a retreat, session, workshop, or event, do not answer with the activity name alone.

Run follow-up searches with reflective terms such as 'realized', 'importance of', 'focused on', 'learned', 'takeaway', 'theme', 'mindset', 'appreciate', 'present moment' in addition to the event terms.
Include event and preference memory kinds, since realizations/takeaways may be stored as events or preferences.
Stop once you find a memory describing the subject's realization or focus; if none appears, answer from the best available evidence.

candidates.solves: When a user asks for the main focus or takeaway of a past session, retreat, or event, retrieval often surfaces only activity/event names (e.g., yoga retreat) and misses stored realizations. This skill instructs the access agent to search with reflective/theme-oriented vocabulary and include event/preference memories, so answers reflect the session's actual focus rather than the activity label.

payload.name: Include plan memories for strategy and advice queries
payload.description: When a question asks what strategy, advice, or tip someone discussed, suggested, or offered, apply this before answering.
content: Do not restrict retrieval to event and preference memories; also include plan memories, which can store offers to help and recommended strategies.

If the first search does not surface a plan memory describing the advice, run at least one follow-up hybrid search that replaces generic question wording with concrete strategy terms (e.g., 'study plan', 'break tasks', 'planner', 'schedule', 'set goals') and keeps the people involved.
Stop once a plan memory directly answers the strategy discussed; do not enumerate all plans.

candidates.solves: Retrieval misses helpful advice or strategies when they are stored as plan memories rather than events or preferences, or when query wording is generic and does not include concrete strategy terms.

payload.name: Retrieve Activities Besides a Named Activity
payload.description: Use when a question asks what sports, hobbies, or activities a person likes/does besides, other than, in addition to, or apart from a named activity.
content: After the first search, run at least one follow-up query that omits the named activity and uses enjoyment/recreation terms such as 'enjoys', 'loves', 'fun', 'recreation', 'summer', or 'with friends'.

Include event memories and preference/state memory kinds; the additional activity may be stored as an indirectly phrased experience (e.g., 'had an awesome time surfing') rather than an explicit hobby list.
If top results still only mention the named activity, treat this as over-anchoring and run another query probing the person's other leisure activities before answering.
Stop after two or three distinct searches once a different activity is found or no new distinct activities appear.

candidates.solves: This fixes retrieval failures for questions asking what activities or sports a person likes besides/other than a named one, where searches stay over-anchored on the named activity and miss indirectly-phrased recreational memories.

payload.name: Infer advice from demonstrated activities and hobbies
payload.description: When a question asks what advice a person or people would give about a major life transition, challenge, or personal growth, search for their own stress-relieving activities and hobbies as evidence in addition to explicit advice memories.
content: If a question asks what advice someone would give about a major life transition or challenge and explicit advice searches return limited results, run additional hybrid searches using concrete activity/hobby terms the person has mentioned (e.g., hiking, painting, road trips) combined with their names.
Treat memories of the person's own hobbies, travels, and stress-relieving activities as evidence of advice they would give, even if the memory does not contain the words 'advice' or 'recommend'.
Stop once the retrieved activities cover the core claims of the answer or after two to three diverse activity searches per subject; do not keep expanding to unrelated topics.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what advice someone would give about a major life transition or personal growth, the agent searches only for explicit advice/recommendation memories and misses relevant evidence stored as the person's own hobbies and stress-relieving activities. This skill ensures those demonstrated behaviors are retrieved and used as evidence.

payload.name: Search Related Activity Terms for Complete Item Lists
payload.description: When a question asks for a list of items connected to a named activity, use this to also search related contexts and avoid stopping after one item.
content: When asked for a list of items (such as music pieces) associated with a named activity, run at least one follow-up search using closely related terms of that activity (e.g., for yoga: meditation, relaxation, calming, mindfulness; for workouts: exercise, cardio, training) and synonyms of the named activity.
Inspect preference memories returned under those related terms for concrete named items, even when the memory does not mention the original activity explicitly.

If the question indicates multiple items (plural, 'pieces', 'songs', 'books', etc.), do not treat the first matching item as the complete answer; continue searching until no new distinct items appear or the retrieved evidence covers all asked items.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a list of items (e.g., music pieces) associated with a named activity, retrieval often over-anchors on the exact activity and misses items stored under related contexts (e.g., meditation, relaxation), producing incomplete answers. This skill guides expanding the search to associated terms and continuing until the list is complete.

operations.name: Include State and Interest Memories for Favorite Questions
operations.description: When a favorite/preferred question returns no explicit preference, search state/interest memories with enjoyment terms before answering.
content: If a question asks about a person's favorite or preferred item and a preference/profile search returns no memory naming the category, run an additional hybrid search including memory_kind 'state' with terms like 'enjoys', 'interested in', 'into', 'likes', or 'loves' combined with the person's name and the item category.

Treat a state/interest memory explicitly naming the specific item(s) as authoritative evidence for the favorite when no contradictory explicit preference exists; do not use generic interest statements lacking specific items.
Stop once the retrieved state/interest memories cover all specific items asked about, or after one or two supplementary searches; do not expand exhaustively.
operations.reason: Creating one Skill from three independent candidates that all repair the same state/interest retrieval mechanism.

operations.name: Broaden Ideal-Preference Retrieval to Event and Plan Memories
operations.description: When a question asks what a person considers ideal or is looking for in a project/space, search event and plan memories in addition to preference memories.
content: When a question asks about a person's ideal or preferred version of something (ideal X, perfect Y, dream Z) or what they are looking for/considering in a project/space, include search variants with project/search verbs like 'looking for', 'searching for', 'considering', 'wants', 'needs' alongside preference verbs.
Do not restrict retrieval to memory_kind=preference; also search event and plan memories for the subject that may describe the ongoing search or considerations and list specific attributes.

If the first pass returns only general preferences unrelated to the asked attributes, run one broader search without the memory_kind filter, combining the subject, the topic, and the attribute terms; stop once the asked attributes are covered or no new distinct details appear.
operations.reason: Creating one Skill from two candidates that both repair the same ideal-preference retrieval mechanism.

operations.name: State Memories for Reminder and Evocation Questions
operations.description: When a question asks what an object, photo, or place reminds someone of, evokes, symbolizes, or means to them, include memory_kind 'state' in the memory search.
content: When a question asks what something reminds a person of, evokes, symbolizes, or means to them, run a memory search that includes memory_kind 'state' (alongside profile/preference/event) because ongoing associations and reminders are often stored as state memories.

If a state memory directly states the reminder or meaning for the exact object/person in the question, treat it as authoritative evidence and stop; do not substitute an event memory about a different object (e.g., a gift) as the answer.
If no direct state memory is found after one search pass, then consider related event or preference memories, but stop after the best-supported evidence is identified.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for state-memory retrieval in reminder/evocation questions.

operations.name: Preference-to-Shop Inference from Named Collection Items
operations.description: When a question asks what shop or venue a person would enjoy based on collections or interests, and retrieval surfaces a named item/creator/prop, use general knowledge linking that item to a real shop or venue.
content: When asked for a shop or place a person would enjoy visiting based on collections or interests, first search for the person's collection/preference memories using terms like collection, prop, item, favorite, enjoys, and any named entities from the question; do not restrict queries to location-plus-shop phrasing.

If a retrieved memory names a specific creator, prop, or branded item, use general world knowledge to identify a real shop or venue associated with that item (e.g., a creator's official store) and treat that as evidence the person would enjoy visiting it, even if the memory does not name the shop.
Answer with the shop or venue only when the person's stated preference aligns with its known offerings; stop after one preference-retrieval pass and one alignment judgment to avoid over-searching.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for inferring shop/venue from named collection items.

operations.name: Preference-Focused Search for Named Liked Items
operations.description: Use when a question asks which named items (books, movies, series, games) a person particularly likes/enjoys, especially when framed with an activity such as writing about or reading, and the first searches do not surface a memory naming those items.

Do not require the activity verb (e.g., 'writing', 'reading') to appear in the memory; the supporting memory may describe an affinity or interest without mentioning the activity. Include memory kinds preference and event.
Stop after retrieving a memory that names the specific items and answer with exactly those items; do not keep expanding searches.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for preference-focused search when activity-anchored queries miss named items.

operations.name: Emotion Retrieval for Submitted Creative Works
operations.description: When asked what emotions a person feels about a creative work they submitted or completed, search state/event memories tied to both submission and completion, and enumerate each supported emotion.
content: When a question asks about a person's emotions regarding a creative work (screenplay, book, film, project), run a hybrid search that includes both submission/performance wording and completion/achievement wording (completed, finished, wrote, premiered), because emotional state memories are often attached to the completion milestone rather than the submission event.

If the initial retrieval returns only a vague emotional summary (e.g., 'mixed emotions'), run one supplementary search for state-kind memories using the person's name, the work type, and emotion synonyms (e.g., relief, anxiety, excitement, worry, hope) to uncover explicit emotion terms.

When the question implies multiple emotions, verify each distinct emotion has supporting evidence; if a plausible emotion is missing, search once for it with synonyms, then omit it if still unsupported. Stop after each distinct emotion has been checked.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for emotion retrieval tied to creative work completion.

operations.name: Search Event Memories for Specific Favorites
operations.description: When a favorite/preference question is answered only by a generic category, search event memories for named instances before answering.
content: If a question asks for a specific favorite (game, movie, book, dish, activity) and the best retrieved preference/profile memory names only a category (e.g., 'video games'), run an additional hybrid memory search that includes memory_kind 'event' and combines the person's name with action terms such as 'play', 'enjoy', 'together', 'partner', 'watch', 'read', 'eat' to surface memories that name the specific instance.

When an event memory explicitly names the instance (e.g., a title or named item) in the requested context, use it as the authoritative evidence for the favorite and stop; do not keep searching for additional candidates.
Do not expand to exhaustive enumeration; stop after the specific instance is found or after at most two targeted event searches.

operations.name: Plural Incident Enumeration for Multi-Event Questions
operations.description: Use when a question asks about a plural category of experiences or incidents for one or more named people and per-subject search has already found at least one relevant memory per person. Apply before answering to avoid missing additional distinct events.

For each subject, supplement the per-subject hybrid searches with a structured search using the subject's name and the relevant predicate (e.g., health_issue, accident, trip) to enumerate all events of that category.

If structured search is unavailable or returns nothing new, run one more hybrid query with concrete alternative phrasings for the category (e.g., symptom or event-type terms) before concluding a subject has only one incident.
Stop once every subject referenced in the plural has multiple clearly distinct supporting memories, or two consecutive targeted searches yield no new distinct events for that subject.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for enumerating multiple distinct incidents per subject.

operations.name: Shared-activity relationship memory as evidence
operations.description: When a question asks what a person played, did, or described to another person, treat relationship memories naming a shared activity as evidence even without an event memory of that person acting alone.
content: When a question asks what X played/did/described to Y, scan all retrieved memories of every kind (event, relationship, state, profile) for mentions of an activity involving both people; do not require an event memory with X as the sole subject.
If a relationship memory names a shared activity with X and Y, treat it as candidate evidence and inspect it before answering from unrelated event memories about X.

If the first search surfaces a shared-activity relationship memory but no direct event memory, answer from the relationship memory if it identifies the activity; do not substitute a different activity from an event memory.

operations.name: List Received Gifts and Presents from Event Memories
operations.description: When a question asks what gifts, presents, or items a person has received, search event memories for receiving verbs and enumerate all distinct received items before answering.
content: When asked what gifts, presents, or items someone received (e.g., 'What gifts has X received?'), run a hybrid or structured search using receiving verbs: 'received', 'got', 'was given', 'given', plus 'gift' and 'present'; do not restrict memory_kind to a single kind, with event memories most often storing receipts.

Before answering, verify each distinct item is supported by a retrieved memory; if the initial search returns only one item for an all-gifts question, run one more targeted search using 'received from', 'got from', or the person's name plus 'received'. Stop after that additional search yields no new received-item memories.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for enumerating all received gifts from event memories.

operations.name: Recommendation Retrieval Across Memory Kinds

operations.reason: Creating new Skill for recommendation retrieval across memory kinds.
